_note: The branching order the lineage chart draws. READ THIS BEFORE TRUSTING IT: a tree is a reading of the literature, not a measurement, and this one is drawn differently from the usual wall chart in two ways. First, a branch leaves its parent at the date the descendant is FIRST SEEN IN THE RECORD — the numbers are already on this map with their sources — and not at a molecular divergence date, which is a different and usually earlier thing. Second, every edge carries how settled it is: 'secure' where the fossils and the dates agree, 'contested' where the literature is arguing, and a contested edge is drawn dashed. A lineage whose position genuinely cannot be drawn is listed in `unplaced` and floats free rather than being given a parent it has not got.

edges.note: Ardipithecus is the oldest hominin known from a skeleton, and whether it is ancestral to Australopithecus or a sister lineage that left no descendants is argued.
The 3.8-million-year-old Woranso-Mille cranium sits between the two, in time and in form, and is read as showing one evolving lineage rather than two.
The South African australopiths come after the east African ones. Which east African species they descend from — or whether the two are one variable species — is not settled.
A mosaic of australopith feet and Homo-like hips and teeth, and its authors argue it sits close to the ancestry of Homo. Others read it as a late australopith side branch.
The heavy-jawed side branch, off an australopith and not off Homo. This is the clearest case on the chart of a lineage that is not our ancestor.

The eastern heavy-jawed form, a sister to the South African one rather than its descendant — boisei is the older of the two, which on its own rules out the other reading. Fifty years of evidence reads the two as one radiation off an australopith.
The stone tools at Lomekwi are 3.3 million years old — older than any fossil that can be placed in the genus. The earlier Homo record here is a category, not a species, and its ancestor is unknown.
OH 7 was reconstructed and found to be more primitive than the flat reconstruction had suggested, and the authors conclude the early genus was several species rather than one.
The Turkana Boy is the first clearly modern body plan in the record. Whether it descends from habilis or from something not yet named is open.
The African and Georgian fossils are read either as one widespread species or as a grade of form that keeps the name. Either way the line runs on through here.
A metre-tall hominin on an island, from about 700,000 years ago — which means an early arrival, on a water crossing, before anyone thought it happened.
A second island hominin, on Luzon, known from hand and foot bones unlike any other species. Its ancestor reached an island it could not have walked to.
The Harbin cranium's affinities are argued: its authors put it closer to sapiens than to Neanderthals, and that reading is disputed.
A Levantine archaic population with tools like those of the sapiens beside it, argued by its authors to be ancestral to Neanderthals.
A small-brained Homo with a modern foot and hand, dated to a time when such a brain should be long gone. Where it belongs is the argument its discovery started.
The oldest securely dated European human, at Gran Dolina — with cut marks on a child's bones. Its dental proteome ties it into the later European lineage.
Sima de los Huesos is read as the root of the Neanderthal line — and its DNA has been read both ways since.
The Neanderthal genome from the Altai and the Sima de los Huesos fossils agree: this is one lineage, in Europe, for 350,000 years.

Neanderthals and Denisovans are sister lineages. They are drawn from the same branch here because Denisova 11 is the child of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father — the two had not yet separated in practice.
An African Middle Pleistocene form, from Bodo and Kabwe, read by many as the ancestor of sapiens and by others as a separate species that left none.
A pan-African origin: the oldest sapiens fossils are in Morocco and Ethiopia, 5,000 km apart and within 15,000 years of each other, so there is no single cradle.

unplaced.why: No fossil, no site and no name. This population is known only from a statistical signal in living West African genomes, so it cannot have a parent drawn on a chart — only the fact that it mixed with Homo sapiens.
